prompt: Why plan a project before writing any code?
choices: Planning makes the finished program run faster
Planning removes the need to test the program later
Planning is only useful for projects with more than one programmer
It decides what the project will and will not do
explain: Without a plan, features get added at random and the project grows until it is too big to finish.

prompt: What is a project proposal?
choices: The finished code, submitted for marking
A written plan of the project's purpose, features and users
A list of the bugs found while testing the finished program
The README file that ships with the project
explain: The proposal is written before the code and acts as the reference you check your work against.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: 0. Write notes, 1. Read chapter, 2. Rest
1. Write notes only
1. Write notes, 2. Read chapter, 3. Rest
It raises a TypeError because enumerate takes one argument
explain: The second argument to enumerate is the number to start counting from, which is how menus number their items from 1.

prompt: What is the difference between a core feature and a nice to have feature?
choices: A core feature is one the project does not work without, a nice to have only improves it
A core feature is easy to build, a nice to have is difficult
A core feature is written first in the file, a nice to have is written last
A core feature is tested, a nice to have does not need testing
explain: Building the core features first means you always have something that works, even if you run out of time.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
def add_task(tasks, name):
    tasks.append({"name": name, "completed": False})
    return tasks

my_tasks = []
add_task(my_tasks, "Buy milk")
add_task(my_tasks, "Walk dog")
print(len(my_tasks), my_tasks[1]["name"])
choices: 2 Buy milk
2 Walk dog
1 Walk dog
It raises an IndexError because the return value was ignored
explain: append changes the list in place, so both tasks land in my_tasks even though the returned list is thrown away.

prompt: Why does a proposal list features that are out of scope?
choices: It shows the marker which features were too hard for you
It reserves those features so nobody else builds them
It is required before you are allowed to use external libraries
It records what you have decided not to build
explain: Naming what you will not do is what keeps a two week project from turning into a two month one.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
def add_task(tasks, name):
    tasks.append(name)

tasks = ["one"]
tasks = add_task(tasks, "two")
print(tasks)
choices: None
['one', 'two']
['two']
It raises a TypeError
explain: The function never returns anything, so it hands back None and the assignment throws the real list away.

prompt: What makes a project goal a SMART goal?
choices: It is short, modern, ambitious, readable and technical
It is simple, memorable, and written in one sentence
It is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time bound
It names the modules, the files and the functions the project will use
explain: Build a command line task manager that adds, lists and completes tasks in two weeks is a SMART goal. Build a task manager is not.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: 7 seven
7 None
It raises a ValueError on the second call
explain: The first call converts cleanly, and the second is caught by the handler, which returns None instead of crashing.

prompt: What belongs in the inputs and outputs section of a proposal?
choices: What data the program takes in and what it produces or displays in return
The names of every variable the program will use
The keyboard shortcuts the program will support
How long each part of the project will take to build
explain: Describing the data flow, such as user types a task then the program saves it and shows the list, clarifies the design early.

prompt: What does this program print?
choices: not a number
cannot divide by zero
It raises a ZeroDivisionError
explain: int("0") succeeds, so the failure happens at the division and the ZeroDivisionError handler is the one that matches.

prompt: Why catch a specific exception such as ValueError instead of catching Exception?
choices: Catching Exception is slower than catching a specific error
Catching Exception is not allowed in a try block
A specific exception can be caught more than once
A broad catch hides bugs you did not expect and makes them look handled
explain: You want the errors you planned for to be handled and everything else to be loud, so you can find it.

prompt: A user typed 3.5 at the prompt. What does this print?
choices: valid
It raises a ValueError
Please enter a whole number.
explain: isdigit is True only when every character is a digit, so a decimal point or a minus sign makes it False.

prompt: Why validate user input before using it?
choices: Validation makes the program use less memory
Validation is the only way to read from the keyboard
Unexpected input would otherwise crash the program partway through its work
Python refuses to run a program that calls input without a check
explain: Checking the value at the point it enters the program means the rest of the code can trust it.

prompt: The user pressed the space bar a few times and then Enter. What does this print?
choices: Input cannot be empty
Saved
Nothing, because the string is not empty
It raises a ValueError
explain: strip removes the spaces and leaves an empty string, which is falsy, so not turns the check True.

prompt: What makes a good feedback message after the user adds an item?
choices: It prints the internal list so the user can see the data structure
It confirms what happened in plain words, such as Task added successfully
It stays silent, because no news is good news
It shows the line number where the item was added
explain: Users need to know their action worked. Dumping raw data or saying nothing at all both leave them guessing.

prompt: The user picks 1, then 9, then 3. What does this print?
choices: Adding task, Goodbye
Adding task, Unknown option, Goodbye, then it keeps looping
Adding task, Unknown option, Goodbye
Unknown option three times
explain: An unrecognised choice falls to the else branch and the menu carries on, and break ends the loop on the exit option.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
def mark_complete(tasks, number):
    if 1 <= number <= len(tasks):
        tasks[number - 1]["completed"] = True
        return True
    return False

tasks = [{"name": "a", "completed": False}, {"name": "b", "completed": False}]
print(mark_complete(tasks, 2))
print(mark_complete(tasks, 3))
choices: True then True
True then False
False then False
True then an IndexError
explain: The range check turns the user's 1 based number into a safe index, and an out of range number is refused instead of crashing.

prompt: What is the job of main.py in a project?
choices: It holds every function in the project, so nothing else is needed
It stores the project's settings and file paths
It contains the tests for the rest of the project
It is the entry point you run, and it calls the functions kept in the other files
explain: One clear starting file tells anyone reading the project where to begin.

prompt: The user asked to delete task 3 from a list of three tasks. What happens?
code:
tasks = ["a", "b", "c"]
number = 3
print(tasks[number])
choices: It raises an IndexError
It prints c
It prints b
It prints None
explain: The list is numbered from 0, so the third task sits at index 2 and the code needs number - 1.

prompt: What is a module in Python?
choices: A .py file holding related functions that other files can import
A folder that contains a project's data files
A function that is used by more than one program
A library that has to be installed with pip
explain: Splitting a project into modules such as utils.py and storage.py keeps related code together.

prompt: These two files sit in the same folder. What does main.py print?
choices: ada lovelace
ada lovelace
Ada Lovelace
It raises a ModuleNotFoundError because utils is not installed
explain: from utils import clean pulls one function out of your own file, and strip then title tidies the text.

prompt: What does this file do when you run it, and what does it do when another file imports it?
choices: It prints running in both cases
It prints running when run directly, and prints nothing when imported
It prints nothing in both cases
It prints running when imported and nothing when run directly
explain: __name__ is only "__main__" in the file you actually started, which is how a module can be imported without side effects.

prompt: Why split a growing project across several files?
choices: Python runs several small files faster than one large one
A single file is limited to about 500 lines
It is the only way to use functions in Python
Related code stays together, so changes and tests stay contained to one part
explain: Structure is about finding and changing code safely, not about speed.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:
def add(a, b):
    """Return the sum of two numbers."""
    return a + b

print(add.__doc__)
choices: None
add(a, b)
Return the sum of two numbers.
It raises an AttributeError because functions have no __doc__
explain: A string on the first line of a function body becomes its docstring, and Python stores it on the function itself.

prompt: What is the difference between a comment and a docstring?
choices: A comment is a note in the source, a docstring can be read at run time
A comment starts with # and a docstring starts with //
A comment is for other people, a docstring is for Python only
A comment can be several lines, a docstring must be one line
explain: Tools such as help() read docstrings, which is why they belong on every function you expect others to call.

prompt: What is wrong with the comment in this code?
code:
# add 1 to count
count = count + 1
choices: It should be placed after the line, not before it
It should be a docstring rather than a comment
Nothing, every line should carry a comment like this
It repeats what the code already says instead of explaining why
explain: Useful comments explain the reason, for example why the count starts at 1 rather than 0.

prompt: What should a comment explain?
choices: What every line does, translated into English
Why the code does what it does, where that is not obvious
Who wrote the line and on what date
Which variables the line will change
explain: Clear code already says what it does. The reasoning behind it is the part that gets lost.

prompt: What does this program print?
code:

age = 25
print(f"[{name:10}][{age:3}]")
explain: A width in a format field pads the value. Text is padded on the right by default and numbers on the left.

prompt: What should a project README contain?
choices: A copy of every function in the project
The full history of every change you made
What the project does, how to install it and how to run it
The list of bugs you have not fixed yet
explain: A README is written for someone who has just found your project and wants to try it in the next two minutes.

Task|Status|
Task<12|Status>8|
Task        |  Status|

prompt: Why spend time formatting a program's output?
choices: Readable output makes the program easier to use
Formatted output runs faster than plain print calls
Python requires every print to use an f-string
It reduces the number of bugs in the program
explain: Presentation is the part of the project a user actually sees, so a little alignment goes a long way.

Total: $13
Total: $12.50

prompt: Why show a list of records as a table rather than one long line each?
choices: Tables use fewer characters than plain lines
Python prints tables faster than it prints lists
Aligned columns let the reader compare the same field down the page
A table is the only way to show more than one field
explain: The whole point of a table is that the eye can run down one column instead of re-reading each line.

[x] a then [x] b
explain: A conditional expression picks the marker, so a finished task shows an x and an unfinished one shows a space.

prompt: What is a sensible order for a short project presentation?
choices: Read the code from top to bottom, then show the program running
List the bugs, then the features, then the code
Introduce the problem, demonstrate the program, explain how it works, then conclude
Show the code, then the proposal, then the plan you started with
explain: Lead with the problem so the audience knows why the demo matters before they see it.

prompt: Which of these is most worth including when you present your project?
choices: A line by line reading of your longest function
What was difficult and how you worked around it
A list of the Python features you chose not to use
An apology for the parts you did not finish
explain: The challenges are where the real learning shows, and they are far more interesting than a code walkthrough.

prompt: What does this program print?

]

prompt: What is the point of reflecting once a project is finished?
choices: It is how the project is graded
You turn the experience into lessons for the next project
It replaces the need to write documentation
It proves the project has no remaining bugs
explain: Reflection is what makes the next project easier, because the lessons are written down rather than forgotten.

prompt: Why put a finished project on GitHub?
choices: It is the only way to keep a backup of your files
It makes the program run on other people's computers automatically
It is required before a project can be called finished
It gives you a public link that shows your code and your README to anyone who asks
explain: A shareable project with a clear README is the most useful thing a beginner can point an employer at.

prompt: What counts as an edge case worth testing in a task manager?
choices: Adding a task with a perfectly ordinary name
Running the program twice in a row
Opening the project in a different editor
Listing tasks when the list is empty
explain: Edge cases sit at the boundary: nothing at all, one item, the very last item, or input the user should not have given.

prompt: What does building a project incrementally mean?
choices: Writing the whole program first and testing it once at the end
Writing every function as a stub, then filling them all in together
Adding one feature at a time and checking it works before starting the next
Adding features in the order they appear in the proposal, no matter how hard
explain: One working feature at a time means you always have something that runs, and a break is easy to trace to your last change.

prompt: What does it mean for a function to do one thing well?
choices: It contains only one line of code
It has a single clear job, so it is easy to name and test
It is called from only one place in the project
It takes only one argument
explain: A function that saves a file and formats a report and asks the user a question is three functions wearing one name.

prompt: Why keep settings such as file paths in named variables at the top of a file?
choices: They can be found and changed in one place
Variables at the top of a file run faster
Python only allows file paths at the top of a file
It stops the settings from being changed by mistake
explain: A value repeated in five places is a value you will one day change in four of them.
